OpenAI must become a safety-first AGI company.

We are long overdue in getting incredibly serious about the implications of AGI.

We must prioritize preparing for them as best we can.

Only then can we ensure AGI benefits all of humanity.
But over the past years, safety culture and processes have taken a backseat to shiny products.

Building smarter-than-human machines is an inherently dangerous endeavor.

OpenAI is shouldering an enormous responsibility on behalf of all of humanity.
Over the past few months my team has been sailing against the wind. Sometimes we were struggling for compute and it was getting harder and harder to get this crucial research done.
These problems are quite hard to get right, and I am concerned we aren't on a trajectory to get there.

I believe much more of our bandwidth should be spent getting ready for the next generations of models, on security, monitoring, preparedness, safety, adversarial robustness, (super)alignment, confidentiality, societal impact, and related topics.

I joined because I thought OpenAI would be the best place in the world to do this research.

However, I have been disagreeing with OpenAI leadership about the company's core priorities for quite some time, until we finally reached a breaking point.
Stepping away from this job has been one of the hardest things I have ever done, because we urgently need to figure out how to steer and control AI systems much smarter than us.

I love my team.

I'm so grateful for the many amazing people I got to work with, both inside and outside of the superalignment team.

OpenAI has so much exceptionally smart, kind, and effective talent.

Going forward, we want to train on harder tasks and decompose the evaluation of tasks instead of the tasks themselves. This way we can empower humans to evaluate our models and give value input even as tasks get very complex, while the model still learns to do the task end-to-end
The model interprets this as she getting asked for her hand in marriage. So when she says yes, it completely misrepresents the plot of the book.

An example from Pride & Prejudice I really liked: the protagonist gets asked “for their hand” at a dance, but the fact that it’s at a dance is not in the model’s context and got left out from summaries of previous pages.

More importantly, we learned a bit about human supervision when decomposing tasks, e.g.:

* Compared to end-to-end training, it’s much easier to debug what the model is doing

* Sometimes there is important context missing when the model only does a small part of the overall task

We combine reward modeling and recursive task decomposition: the model summarizes a few pages at the time, then summarizes the summaries, and so on. The result is a model that actually writes plausible summaries of entire books, even matching average human quality 5% of the time.

I'm very interested in techniques for supervising models to do tasks that are difficult for humans to evaluate.

To study this, we trained a model on summarizing entire books!

text: Ideally the model should always write the best code, no matter how buggy the context. These kind of alignment problems are what we're trying to solve!
What is surprising is that the effect is quite strong: subtly buggy context degrades performance equivalent to a ~10x smaller model.

This is not surprising, given the nature of the training distribution: if a file contains bad code, it's more likely to contain more bad code, so guessing that bad code will follow is a good strategy for the model.

There are a lot of exciting things in the Codex paper, but my favorite titbit is the misalignment evaluations by @BethMayBarnes: Subtly buggy code in the context makes the model more likely to write buggy code, and this discrepancy gets larger as the models get bigger! https://t.co/nPiFngBW9t
